title: Public trust doctrine

definition.text: The principle that the state holds certain resources, such as the shore between high and low tide, in trust for public use, whoever owns the land beside them.

facts.text: It goes back to Roman law, which held air, flowing water, the sea and the seashore to be common to all and not open to ownership.
It passed into English law and later into the common law of the United States, where it covers tidal and navigable waters and the minerals and animals in them.
It has been used to claim public interest in oil under tidal lands and to stop private ownership of fish stocks and shellfish beds.
Some countries have used it to protect natural resources as a human right, and protections are spreading to a global scale.

notes: Much of the page is US state law; kept for its general principle and Roman origins.

definition.text: A Roman law idea of things common to all humankind, such as air, running water, the sea and its shores, that came before modern ideas of the commons.

facts.text: The Institutes of Justinian codified it in the 6th century.
It differs from res publica, public property managed by government, since common things are for everyone to use and enjoy.
In environmental law it means the state is trustee of shared natural resources and cannot sell them into private hands.
Fish and mammals on the high seas are examples, and the rules for Antarctica and for space law were built on it.

definition.text: Paul Samuelson's rule for the best amount of a public good: provide more as long as the total of everyone's extra benefit is at least the extra cost of providing it.

facts.text: Formally, the sum of all consumers' marginal rates of substitution equals the economy's marginal rate of transformation between the public good and a private good.
For a private good, by contrast, each consumer's own valuation is set equal to the cost of producing one more unit.
Because everyone enjoys a public good at once, individual demands are added together vertically, so the rule extends supply and demand from private to public goods.
If two people would pay $200 and $100 for a park costing $225, its $300 total value leaves a $75 surplus, so it should be built.
Samuelson stressed that people have reasons to understate their valuations, which makes applying the rule hard in practice.

definition.text: A situation where people act for short-term personal gain in a way that, in the long run, leaves the whole group worse off.

facts.text: John Platt introduced the term in a 1973 paper, applying behavioral psychology to Hardin's tragedy of the commons.
Social traps are blamed for overfishing, overgrazing in the Sahel, rainforest destruction and, above all, climate change.
Choosing a car over public transport is a social trap: comfort now, more greenhouse gas emissions later.
Platt proposed rewards for green behavior and penalties such as pollution taxes as ways out.

definition.text: A situation where each person does better by acting selfishly whatever others do, yet everyone would do best if all cooperated.

facts.text: Robyn Dawes coined the term a few years after Platt, to cover both social traps and commons dilemmas.
There are three main kinds: large-scale dilemmas, commons (resource) dilemmas and public goods dilemmas.
Uncertainty about others' actions or about the resource discourages cooperation, but a trustworthy leader who manages the resource fairly can restore it.

title: Tragedy of the anticommons

definition.text: The mirror image of the tragedy of the commons: when a resource has many owners who can each block its use, it ends up underused.

facts.text: Michael Heller introduced the term in a 1998 article, after seeing empty shops in post-communist Eastern European cities where too many parties held rights over each space.
Early aviation patents held by the Wright brothers and Glenn Curtiss blocked each other until the government created a patent pool in World War I.
Housing shortages in many western cities have been described this way, since zoning lets many stakeholders block new homes.
Remedies include eminent domain and patent pools or other licensing bodies.

contested_note: Heller and Eisenberg argue biological patents create an anticommons, while others, citing surveys of scientists, say they have not.
